description: Our team is developing an interactive space mission design game that allows users to plan and simulate missions across the Solar System. By combining mathematical modelling, orbital mechanics, and interactive web development, we aim to create an engaging platform where players make decisions about spacecraft, trajectories, fuel, budgets, and mission objectives. We bring skills in mathematics, programming, and problem-solving, and welcome creative collaborators.
summary: DELTA-V is a browser game where you plan, build and fly a complete space mission. Players pick one of six missions (Moon, Mars, Venus, an asteroid sample return, Europa and Titan), choose science instruments that match the mission's goals, pick a launch date from launch windows computed from real NASA JPL planet positions, and size the power, radio, engine and rocket. Live meters show how every choice changes cost, weight, power and expected science. Then they fly it: they time the launch, correct the course, hold the engine to brake into orbit, and photograph science targets, while solar storms, faults and discoveries test their decisions. A final report grades the mission and explains which choices caused each success or failure. It turns the abstract trade-offs of mission design into something students can play and understand in minutes, with a built-in guide for beginners and no install or account needed.
details:
What it does: DELTA-V lets anyone run a space mission from proposal to final report.

1) Choose a mission: six targets, from an easy lunar ice prospector to a Titan explorer, each with weighted science goals and a cost cap.

2) Build the spacecraft in a 3D hangar, one question at a time: mission type (flyby, orbiter, aerobraking, lander, entry probe or sample return), instruments, launch date, solar or nuclear power, radio dish, engine, radiation shielding, backup computers, safety margins and rocket. The 3D model changes as parts are added, and four meters (money, weight, power, science) update live. A design review blocks designs that could not fly.

3) Fly it: time the launch window, steer a mid-course correction, hold the engine to brake into orbit (too short and you fly past, too long and you waste fuel), and snap science targets in a photo pass. Solar flares, computer faults, radiation damage and discoveries ask for decisions along the way.

4) Learn from the result: a grade, a mission patch, and plain-language lessons tied to the player's own choices.

How it works: planet positions come from NASA JPL's Keplerian elements. Launch windows come from a Lambert solver (about 10,000 solutions per launch chart). Fuel follows the rocket equation, solar power and radio data rate fall with distance squared, and cost, schedule and risk models react to the design. A guide character (Nova) shows beginners what to press, with "Pick for me" and "Build it all for me" buttons. An Engineer view shows every number for advanced users.

Benefits and impact: no install and no account, so it runs on school computers and phones. It teaches why spaceflight is hard and why margins matter through play, in a single class period.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js (3D), HTML Canvas, Web Audio, Node.js (build script and automated tests that fly 480 simulated missions), GitHub Pages hosting. Built with help from Claude (Anthropic).

Next: multi-planet gravity-assist tours, a class leaderboard, and missions based on Space Agency Partner projects.
